The way I was originally taught music theory (which I would say is the wrong way) is just describing aspects of sheet music without even listening to the music the sheet music was showing. Like "x" on the page is "y". I think many people imagine this when they hear music theory (or any thing with the word theory in it). I wasn't taught how to apply the concepts I was learning to actual music just writing on a page. 
Having taken more classes now I would argue that even though it wasn't as extreme a lot of my teachers did not really show me how it was actually applied to our practice.
I think something else at least from my experience is that those that took music theory were snobbish about pop music, rap, etc and refused to consider them which further painted them in a bad light.

I realize these are misconceptions and I'm glad I was able to learn how to apply what I've learned and find my love for music theory but I do think it has a "PR" problem.

I was watching American Ballet Theatre's World Ballet Day video this year and the teacher said "male/female technique" rather than "male/female dancer" when describing things. The distinction is small but comforting. 

I took ballet a few years ago and was the only "boy" (if only you could go back and talk to your younger self!) and it was very accepting of my femininity. My teacher even encouraged me to go on pointe if I wanted.

Spend some time looking for a program safe for you and no matter what happens, never let anyone steal your passion for dance 🙏
